overview: Teenek people speak a Mayan language and live especially in San Luis Potosí and Veracruz. Their history belongs to the diverse Huasteca region, whose inhabitants included several peoples. The 1492 to 1500 outline is a partial historical map label, not a single unified kingdom or the boundary of all living Teenek communities.

periods.title: Earlier towns and craft households
periods.summary: Tamtoc developed organized public spaces and substantial houses, including evidence interpreted as specialized craft production.

periods.title: Regional centres and river routes
periods.summary: Huastec builders expanded towns and ceremonial buildings, including the layered mound at Las Flores.

periods.title: Conquest and colonial land pressure
periods.summary: Spanish colonization brought violence, encomiendas, cattle estates and growing pressure on Indigenous land.

periods.title: Continuing communities and languages
periods.summary: Teenek communities maintain their language across San Luis Potosí and Veracruz.

items.text: At Las Flores, in present-day Tampico, one surviving mound measures about 36 metres across and 6 metres high. Excavators identified 26 successive floors inside it. Builders repeatedly enlarged and resurfaced a structure that now looks like one hill: archaeology can read its layers almost like pages.

Las Flores builders protected earthen structures with lime coatings and crushed shell. INAH describes a thick shell layer treated with liquid lime and polished to help keep water out of the earth beneath. Coastal materials offered a practical answer to the problem of rain soaking a building.

Tamohi stood beside the Tampaón River and occupied roughly 210 hectares. Its surroundings supported maize, beans, squash and chilli, as well as cotton. Food crops and useful fibres belonged to the same regional economy, while the river connected settlements and supplied a route through the landscape.

Inside Tamohi’s painted altar, excavators found built benches and a central form with coloured decoration. The surviving figures have been interpreted as priests or gods. Visiting a ruined platform today can hide an important part of its original appearance: its surfaces once carried vivid painted scenes.

The sandstone sculpture called the Huastec Adolescent is 145 centimetres tall and came from Tamohi. The museum notes carved teeth, pierced ears and nose, and a hand with a hole that may once have held a banner. Details of dress and display survive even when the original accessories do not.

A smaller figure appears on the Adolescent’s back, and designs cover his body. Scholars have proposed different divine identities, including a maize deity and Quetzalcoatl carrying the Sun. The scene should not be treated as a photograph of ordinary childcare; its meaning remains debated.

At Tamtoc, channels and water-storage features were built around springs. Archaeologist Estela Martínez Mora connects these works with rituals concerning life and death. An offering near a spring included the sculpture now called the Scarred Woman. Water was both a daily resource and part of a sacred landscape.

A Tamtoc residential complex excavated in 2015 had generous space and elaborate finishes. Martínez Mora suggests that it housed specialists who worked stone and shell during the town’s earlier urban period. A carefully finished house can reveal something about skilled work and social standing, alongside its rooms and walls.

INPI describes Teenek families connected through mutual help. These networks include extended relatives, friends and ritual kin. Neighbours and family ties help organize work, while communal faena brings people together for tasks of shared interest.

A modern gathering may include zacahuil: maize dough with meat and chilli, wrapped in banana or papatla leaves and baked. INPI records it at celebrations and market days. This is food made for sharing, rather than a tiny snack to slip into your pocket.

Mexica rulers conquered parts of the Huasteca before Spanish invasion. During the sixteenth century, Spanish violence, encomiendas and cattle estates disrupted Indigenous communities. Land pressure continued after the initial fighting. These changes did not erase the people whose descendants still live in the region.

“Nenek” means “Hello”. INALI prints this greeting in its western Tének phrase guide and credits Luis Flores Martínez and Esiquio Martínez Cruz for the text and recordings. It is a documented modern language sample from San Luis Potosí, written in Latin letters.

In 2016, INALI presented a Tének edition of The Little Prince at the National Museum of Anthropology’s book fair. Language promoter Telésforo del Ángel Domínguez, from San Francisco in Chontla, Veracruz, spoke about reading literature in one’s own language. Contemporary publishing adds new books to a living language.

ending.text: The map’s 1500 endpoint does not mark the disappearance of Teenek people. Communities in San Luis Potosí and Veracruz continue to speak their language, and modern publishing creates new reading opportunities. Ancient towns changed or were abandoned, while the history of their wider region continued.
